transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-20 16:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Claire Holden (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Morris (Redwood CSM), Markus Lee (CTO, Orion), Ana Ruiz (Head of MLOps), Jordan Park (Infra), Priya Narang (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Goal: scope a 4-week POC to evaluate hosting modes (Hosted API vs Dedicated reserved capacity vs Private/VPC) for Orion's doc understanding + RAG pipeline.
- Discussed success criteria (latency & cost targets), workload sizing, security constraints, benchmark plan, and timeline.
- Next step: Redwood to run perf baseline; customer to share traces + security checklist.

Topics touched: success criteria, throughput sizing, p95 latency targets, KV cache behavior, data residency, SOC2/SAML, rollout plan and timelines, cost tradeoffs, fallback strategies.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Claire: hey everyone thanks for joining — um i think we have about 45 minutes — quick intro round, i am claire from redwood, ravi is our se who will do the perf bits, lena on cs — and over to orion?
[00:12] Markus: hey — markus here — thanks, we are eager to align on hosting options. short primer: we run a RAG pipeline serving analysts and internal apps, about 1200 active users, peak concurrent queries around 45 to 60, avg prompt ~550 tokens but some longer at 2k tokens.
[00:28] Ana: yeah and we have a mix of short chat style and long-document extraction. our success criteria are fairly concrete: latency, cost, and no data egress outside our VPC for certain docs.
[00:40] Claire: perfect — that lets us frame hosted vs dedicated vs private. ravi, want to kick into sizing implications?
[00:45] Ravi: sure — so first high-level: Hosted API is fastest to start, we can stand up endpoints in minutes, but cost per token tends to be higher and there are multi-tenant constraints; Dedicated buys you reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput; Private (VPC or on-prem) gives you control for data residency and strict network egress — but takes most time to provision and onboard.
[01:10] Jordan: can you quantify "predictable throughput"? we need headroom for 2x peak bursts coming from daily jobs.
[01:17] Ravi: for a typical 7B-ish quantized model on one dedicated GPU pool you can see roughly X qps for short responses; with continuous batching our runtime usually improves tokens/sec at scale. for your mix (avg 600 tokens) i'd ballpark needing 4-6 high-memory GPUs to meet p95 < 700ms for most requests if you want <60 concurrent. but that's rough — we should run a benchmark with your exact prompts.
[01:43] Markus: that aligns with internal back-of-envelope. can you say more about batching impact on latency? sometimes batching adds jitter we can't tolerate.
[01:52] Ravi: good point — continuous/streaming batching in our runtime tries to avoid latency cliffs: small batches for low concurrency, grows when we see more parallelism. p50 vs p95 behavior depends heavily on request length distribution. in short: batching reduces cost per token but can add p95 tail if concurrency is spiky.
[02:11] Ana: our SLOs are p50 < 250ms and p95 < 900ms for the shorter chat flows; long-document jobs are allowed higher latency up to 6s. is that achievable on hosted?
[02:24] Claire: hosted can achieve that for many configs — with caching, prefix reuse, and tuned model variants. but if you need network egress control or dedicated throughput guaranteed, Dedicated or Private are better.
[02:35] Priya: security check — we have documents in scope that cannot leave our VPC and some PII; SOC2 is required, SAML SSO, and KMS-managed keys for model inputs/outputs at rest. can the hosted plan meet that?
[02:50] Claire: hosted — we have SOC2 and support customer-managed keys via integration, but full VPC egress control is limited; we offer Private for full VPC and on-prem installs. dedicated can be done in a private network if we set up dedicated peering / cross-account VPC.
[03:05] Jordan: how long to get a Private deployment? we tried a vendor who quoted 8-12 weeks and that derailed us.
[03:12] Ravi: typical Private on our side is 4-6 weeks after contract + infra access; Dedicated provisioning (reserved capacity) is usually 2-3 weeks to get predictable pools and autoscaling rules. Hosted is immediate. but note onboarding and security reviews can add time on your end.
[03:28] Markus: ok timeline looks doable. next, benchmarks — what will you need from us to run the perf test?
[03:35] Ravi: ideally: a 72-hour sample traffic trace with timestamps, 5-10 representative prompts across your short and long families, and an auth token for a sandbox dataset or anonymized payloads. then we'll run baseline runs: 50 qps and a burst window test to simulate 2x bursts. we'll measure p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and cost estimate.
[03:56] Ana: we can provide traces but need to scrub PII first. is synthetic okay?
[04:01] Ravi: synthetic is fine as long as it matches token distribution and sequence length. sometimes content affects decoding length but distribution is most important.
[04:09] Claire: for the POC success criteria, should we capture them now so they're in the scope doc?
[04:14] Markus: yeah let's do that. primary success criteria: 1) adherence to latency SLOs for short flows (p50 < 250ms, p95 < 900ms), 2) cost target under $X per 1k tokens (we'll provide an internal target number), 3) security: no uncontrolled egress for sensitive docs, SOC2 + KMS compliance, 4) stability: >=99.5% availability during benchmark window.
[04:40] Priya: add: audit logs and per-request tracing with retention 90 days minimum — we need that for our audit team.
[04:48] Lena: quick note — Redwood Console supports token-level cost breakdowns and tracing hooks; we can include that in the demo.
[04:55] Jordan: curious about the KV cache you mentioned — how would that work for our RAG pipeline? we have a mid-size index and a lot of repeated prefixes.
[05:04] Ravi: KV cache is prefix-level caching of generated context and attention caches; for RAG it helps more on multi-turn sessions with repeated doc context. it reduces token compute and latency for repeated queries, but warm-up time matters. cache hit rates will be highly workload dependent.
[05:20] Ana: so in hosted, cache might be multi-tenant and warm across customers? any risk?
[05:26] Ravi: caches are isolated per customer on Dedicated and Private; hosted has scoped caches and opt-in caching controls — we can choose not to persist shared caches for sensitive workloads.
[05:36] Markus: pricing — Claire, we need a hosted estimate and a dedicated commitment outline. also curious about fallback policies if capacity is constrained.
[05:44] Claire: we'll send a cost comparison sheet — in short: hosted is pay-as-you-go; Dedicated is a commit (monthly or annual) with burst capacity, we can align commit to predicted throughput. fallback policies: smart routing — if Dedicated pool is saturated we can failover to hosted variants with rate limits and token caps to preserve service. that's configurable.
[06:05] Priya: legal/procurement question: do we need to accept a data processing addendum? and how long until we can get a contract redline?
[06:13] Claire: yes DPA + standard security addenda; we usually can turn around initial redlines in 7-10 business days depending on complexity. procurement often starts once POC signals green.
[06:22] Jordan: for benchmarks, what model variants will you test? we sometimes prefer smaller models for cost, but need to preserve quality.
[06:29] Ravi: we'll test a matrix: first-tier open model (quantized 7B-ish), a 13B variant, and a trimmed 70B variant for accuracy/latency tradeoffs. we'll also test warm vs cold KV cache and a few quantization profiles — Redwood Optimize will give recommendations keyed to your workload.
[06:46] Ana: accuracy regression is a risk — we will need baseline evals. can you run evals tied to prompt sets?
[06:52] Ravi: yes, we can hook the same prompt families into eval harnesses and measure top-line metrics: exact-match, F1, hallucination flags. we'll produce a small regression dashboard.
[07:02] Markus: great. curious about private deployment options — we have an air-gapped environment for a subset of docs. would Redwood support an on-prem package?
[07:10] Claire: yes we do an on-prem package for regulated workloads; it requires more ops time and typically an on-site runbook, but it's doable. timeline and cost are higher vs VPC-only.
[07:20] Priya: we will need to see network diagrams and KMS flow. please send those.
[07:24] Claire: noted — we'll attach the security architecture and SOC2 docs.
[07:28] Jordan: any gotchas around streaming responses and function/tool-calling? we call internal tools post-generation.
[07:34] Ravi: streaming is supported across hosting modes; function/tool-calling works but Private gives you the lowest latency to local tool endpoints. hosted can call webhooks but if you want no egress, Private is the option.
[07:47] Ana: timeline recap — we want to run the POC in early March. is that feasible?
[07:51] Claire: yes — propose: Week 0 (this week): scope and sign POC statement. Week 1: provide traces + prompts, Redwood runs baseline smoke tests; Week 2: 48-hour perf window + tuning; Week 3: run accuracy/regression evals and security review; Week 4: wrap-up, decision and cost/rollout plan.
[08:12] Markus: that timeline works if benchmarks align.
[08:16] Claire: ok i'll capture this in the scope doc and send with pricing. any final questions?
[08:21] Priya: one last — token retention and logs: can we configure retention policy shorter than 30 days? we need logs kept for 90 but payload retention shorter.
[08:29] Lena: yes retention is configurable per account with different tiers; we will include that in the security pack.
[08:33] Jordan: good. thanks everyone.
[08:36] Claire: thanks — quick recap of next steps then: 1) customer to send traces + prompts (Markus/Ana) 2) Redwood to run 48-hr perf and share metrics (Ravi) 3) Redwood to send pricing + security docs (Claire) 4) Priya to confirm any blocker items from security checklist. we'll tentatively book a results review on 2026-03-05.
[08:56] Markus: thanks, see you then.
[09:00] (call ends)
